latest_articles.journal: Annals of the International Communication Association
latest_articles.title: Toward a novel framework of understanding the relationship between social media use and political knowledge: a systematic literature review
latest_articles.abstract: While recent quantitative research finds little evidence that citizens learn about politics from social media, it is unclear whether studies adequately capture platform complexity and often fragmented understandings of political knowledge. Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically reviewed 78 papers that assess the quantitative association between social media use and political knowledge. Our critical assessment of how such studies conceptualize and operationalize social media use and political knowledge revealed a dual mismatch. First, social media use is often measured via general frequency, overlooking specific content (beyond “news”), actors (e.g., influencers), platforms (beyond Facebook/Twitter), and exposure modes (e.g., incidental). Second, knowledge measures remain conservative, focusing on institutional facts while neglecting issue-specific and noninstitutional topics. We propose a novel 3-dimensional framework and methodological pathways to address key limitations in the dominant normative tradition of studying the relationship between social media and political learning.
affiliations: School of Social Sciences, Hasselt University , Hasselt,
Media, Information & Persuasion Lab, Department of Communication Science, KU Leuven , , Leuven
Media Psychology Lab, Department of Communication Science, KU Leuven , Leuven,
Department of Communication, University of Vienna , Vienna,
Department of Political Science, University of Antwerp , Antwerp,

latest_articles.title: Digital Agency Tools: A Way to Buffer the Negative Effects of Excessive Phone Use?
latest_articles.abstract: In times of ubiquitous smartphone use, most users adopt one or more self-imposed rules regarding their device usage, also known as voluntary digital disconnection. Drawing on the Integrative Model of Mobile Media Use and Need Experiences (IM³UNE), this study provides empirical evidence on the adoption of digital agency tools and their potential in mitigating ill-being (depression, anxiety, and stress) associated with excessive smartphone use. We conducted a quota-based online survey involving n = 384 ( M age = 49.6) smartphone users in Flanders (Belgium). The results provide a systematization of different digital agency tools, showing they are widely used among adults. Importantly, we provide preliminary evidence on their potential in buffering ill-being due to excessive smartphone use. For users of detox apps and in-app well-being features, the associations between excessive use and ill-being were nonsignificant, unlike for nonusers of these tools. For users of default device settings, such as iOS ScreenTime, there were no differences. Our findings contribute to theory by applying and empirically testing critical elements of the IM³UNE model. Empirically, our findings indicate the importance of studying different types of tools, as they do not appear to be equally beneficial.
affiliations: Department of Communication Science, Media Psychology Lab, KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium.
Department of Communication, University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Business and Technical Communication
latest_articles.title: Learning How to Write as a Cyborg
latest_articles.abstract: Discussions of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) focus on describing AI as either a tool or a collaborator. Such discussions do not fully grasp GenAI's transformative impact. This article proposes a model of cyborg learning that outlines the skills necessary for using GenAI effectively: background knowledge, critical evaluation of AI output, and rhetorical integration of AI output. Presenting multiple use cases from the literature in technical and professional communication and the author's own experience, the article illustrates how to write as a cyborg.

latest_articles.title: Clarifying the role of authenticity in online self-effects: examining authentic cognition and authentic self-expression
latest_articles.abstract: Research on self-effects (i.e., how communicators influence themselves) has shown that people can change their self-perceptions, cognitions, attitudes, and behaviors according to their public online self-presentations. Identity shift theorizing has argued that self-presentations have to be authentic to elicit the greatest self-effects. The present study posited that authentic self-presentations should be conceptualized as two different components—authentic cognition and authentic self-expression—understood from a communicator’s point of view. In a between-subjects experiment, participants were instructed to publicly self-present on their actual social media accounts in one of three ways that correspond to descending levels of authentic cognition and authentic self-expression: with mindfulness (with awareness, balance, and acceptance), with facticity (being purely factual and unemotional), or with self-glorification (with exaggerations and embellishments). Results showed that participants who self-presented mindfully experienced less toxic positivity than those who self-glorified, and less toxic positivity was associated with greater commitment to their self-presentations and greater recalled enjoyment. However, the more narcissistic participants were, the more they enjoyed self-glorification than self-presenting mindfully. Therefore, the study showed that authenticity shaped self-effects associated with public online self-presentation and extended self-effects theorizing to cognitive-affective evaluations of recalled experience.
affiliations: Wee Kim Wee School of Communication and Information, Nanyang Technological University , Singapore,

latest_articles.title: Du Boisian practice & thought for journalism studies
latest_articles.abstract: W.E.B. Du Bois was a massively important 20th century journalist and intellectual. However, his journalistic practice and social theorizing are not often retrieved by journalism studies scholars as analytic resources. To make the case for his utility, I first demonstrate how Du Bois alters scholarly analyses of the 1619 Project that stress the effort’s novelty. In contrast, I situate the 1619 Project in a Du Boisian tradition marked by empiricism and positive propaganda, a combination which swims against professional journalists’ emic understandings of objectivity. I then tour moments of Du Bois’s career that show how he theorized processes of interest to journalism scholars, including his analysis of the Black press and his wider theorizing of discursive culture and its impact on habitual racism. I conclude by contrasting Du Bois to his contemporary and correspondent Walter Lippmann.

latest_articles.title: From normative principles to epistemic governance: A workflow-based analysis of European journalism ethics in datafied environments
latest_articles.abstract: Data journalism has received limited attention in journalism ethics, where it is often assumed that established normative principles apply directly to data-driven practices. However, data journalism relies on complex data processes that introduce distinct epistemic challenges related to bias, interpretation, and accountability. This study examines data journalism ethics as a form of epistemic governance embedded across key stages of the data journalism workflow, from data gathering to data visualisation, drawing on a thematic analysis of 37 ethical codes from 32 European countries. The findings show that, while ethical codes consistently articulate principles such as accuracy, fairness, and transparency, they rarely operationalise them in relation to methodological decisions shaping data-driven reporting. The epistemic governance framework serves as a bridge between data journalism ethics and AI ethics, as many AI-related ethical challenges originate in data practices and are intensified by automation.
affiliations: Department of Information Science and Media Studies, University of Bergen
Centre for Media and Journalism Studies, University of Groningen

latest_articles.title: War or humanitarian crisis? A framing analysis of flemish media coverage of Gaza in 2023 and 2024
latest_articles.abstract: This study analyzes how the Gaza conflict is framed in Flemish media, focusing on articles from De Standaard (DS) and Het Laatste Nieuws (HLN). Coverage was examined during three key moments over 1 year: the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023, the bombings of Rafah starting May 6, 2024, and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant on November 21, 2024. Using an existing framing matrix, the study investigated (1) which frames were used, (2) how they differed between newspapers, and (3) whether they shifted across time. The results show that the human interest frame, followed by the war frame, dominated coverage in both newspapers. In the first two periods, the three most common frames were similar across DS and HLN. Only in the third period (November 2024) did the most frequently used frames differ. Over time, different framings emerged for each event, although human interest and war frames remained consistently present. Both outlets relied primarily on Western sources, leading to a potential source bias. Compared to DS, HLN presented events in a less nuanced way, which is expected from a popular newspaper. This study offers new insight into Flemish media representations of the Gaza conflict, a largely underexplored subject.

latest_articles.title: Vaccine framing dynamics: Media influence, social media sharing, and public sensemaking during a crisis
latest_articles.abstract: During crises like the COVID-19 pandemic, information dissemination and sensemaking processes profoundly shape public perceptions. This study investigates the intricate interplay between media framing, social media sharing, and individual reinterpretation of COVID-19 vaccination news on Facebook. Analyzing 1957 articles from The New York Times (NYT) over 2 years, the research delves into news framing dynamics and their influence on Facebook sharing patterns. Findings reveal eight frames used by journalists, with a focus on scientific development, political controversy, and societal impact. Notably, the anti-vaccination frame received the highest number of shares per article. I also explored the content of the individual shares examining how individuals changed the information provided by the NYT during the sharing process.
affiliations: Department of Public Relations and STEM Translational Communication Center, University of Florida, Gainesville, USA

latest_articles.title: ‘Not for me’: Reasons for (non)participation in science communication activities on Artificial Intelligence in the Netherlands
latest_articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence operates in a social context and affects everyone. Organizing science communication and engagement activities on the topic for all groups in society is therefore recommendable. However, research shows that mainly higher educated, already engaged citizens participate in science communication activities. To address this gap, our study collected insights from underrepresented citizens in the Netherlands regarding their views on and participation in science communication activities related to artificial intelligence. Using semi-structured interviews (n = 19), we qualitatively explored reasons for (non)participation. Participants knew more about AI than they initially reported, and worldviews were evoked in expressing both concerns and curiosity about AI. AI was deemed relevant but news about the topic was avoided due to a lack of trust. Non participation in engagement or communication activity was driven by both practical and social barriers. Following participants’ advice, we suggest a personal approach could help to make these activities more inviting.
affiliations: Communication Science, University of Twente, Enschede, The Netherlands
Marketing and Communication, University of Twente, Enschede, The Netherlands

latest_articles.title: Identifying Alternatives to Retraction of Controversial Research Findings
latest_articles.abstract: Although academic journals have historically prioritized dissemination of accurate information, some journals now consider information hazards in editorial policies. Editors may reject or retract papers based on their perceived potential to impose societal harms. Such editorial policies have received pushback from scholars seeing such policies as impediments to effective science communication. Across four experiments, we tested how both scientists and everyday people view harm-based retractions and alternatives to retraction for addressing controversy. Academic researchers and lay perceivers disapproved of retractions based on information hazards, preferring commentaries, replications, adversarial collaborations, and even inaction . We offer policy recommendations for science communication.
affiliations: The University of Southern Mississippi, Hattiesburg, USA
New College of Florida, Sarasota, USA
Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, Philadelphia, PA, USA

latest_articles.title: Kaleidoscopic contradictions: Ecological paradoxes in AI-powered interactive digital narrative
latest_articles.abstract: This study aims to analyze the ecological contradictions inherent in artificial intelligence-supported interactive digital narrative systems. Drawing on theoretical frameworks such as post-digital aesthetics, media ecology, and critical environmental studies, the research analyzes case studies of interactive designs that question contradictory realities from perspectives including artificial intelligence and the environment, ecological media infrastructures, post-anthropocentric narratives, data criticism, and ethics. While praised for offering personalized and immersive narrative experiences, these works cause high environmental costs due to their reliance on unsustainable infrastructures. Although ecology-focused, they are mostly produced within technological systems that materially undermine this theme and are circulated through these systems. However, these material realities are often overshadowed by the visually impressive presentation of the narratives, leading to a new kind of ecological blindness. In this context, the contradictions of kaleidoscopic narratives in the creation of interactive art are questioned, and the importance of rethinking AI-supported digital narratives not only at the content level but also in terms of production and distribution infrastructures within an environmentally ethical context is discussed. The research offers suggestions on questions such as how to integrate design criticism and practice to reduce the energy costs of digital narrative and minimize its ecological impact, how to establish carbon-aware design methodologies and accountability frameworks, and how to incorporate environmental calculations into the production workflow, and it argues for the necessity of considering environmental costs as well as the need to move beyond a profit loss focused mindset as one of the most important problems of digital representation forms. Finally, calling for a new paradigm shift in the field of culture, the research emphasizes the importance of adopting eco-materialist paradigms, away from human-centeredness, for truly sustainable and ecologically sensitive digital narratives.

latest_articles.title: Podcast talk: Knowledge-making through voice, circulation, and listening
latest_articles.abstract: This article argues that podcasting should be understood not merely as a means of disseminating knowledge, but as a knowledge-making practice in its own right. Drawing on theories of broadcast talk, mediated address, and communication as dissemination, it develops the concept of podcast talk to examine how podcasts organise knowledge through voice, sequence, intimacy, circulation, and listening. Rather than presenting a bounded empirical case study, the article synthesises existing podcast scholarship on narrative nonfiction, independent podcasting, journalism, counterpublics, intimacy, host authority, and listening contexts. It identifies three ways podcasting produces knowledge. First, by circulating voices and accounts through platforms and publics. Second, by reshaping expertise and authority through vocal presence, lived experience, and relational trust. Third, by making knowledge meaningful through embodied, affective listening encounters. At the same time, the article treats podcasting as an ambivalent epistemic form, whose intimacy and authority can also intensify misplaced trust, misinformation, and unequal visibility. Podcasting moves knowledge off the page by making communicative form central to knowledge-making practice.
affiliations: School of Communication Studies, Auckland University of Technology,

latest_articles.title: An integrative approach to predicting student motivation
latest_articles.abstract: This study examined the extent to which demographics (sex), personality traits (extraversion and neuroticism), cognitive dispositions (resilience and locus of control), social-personal dispositions (Machiavellianism), and instructional communicative behaviors (teacher confirmation and student communication satisfaction) predict state student motivation. Drawing on an integrative framework and informed by Self-Determination Theory, data from 367 university students in the United States were analyzed using path analysis. Results revealed that, collectively, these variables explained 78% of the variance in student motivation; however, only instructional communicative behaviors (responding to questions, demonstrating interest, communication satisfaction), resilience, and Machiavellianism emerged as significant predictors. These findings indicate that while individual differences contribute to motivation, communicative classroom behaviors play a particularly central and proximal role in shaping student motivation, underscoring the importance of instructor–student interaction in higher education.

latest_articles.title: Mesh, Texture, Meta-data: A Media Archaeology of 3D file formats
latest_articles.abstract: This article develops a media-archaeological account of three-dimensional imaging formats, focusing on .obj, .stl and .ply. It treats the .obj folder as a format assemblage in which spatial data (mesh), surface data (texture) and instructional data (material/metadata) remain technically separable but become visible as a coherent image only through software coordination. A selective history of 3D formats shows how industrial demands for storage, interoperability and portability have shaped the appearance and circulation of spatial images. Case studies of Sophie Kahn, Hito Steyerl and Alan Warburton examine how artists isolate, preserve and restage the seams of this layered construction. Kahn exposes the inference and repair required to turn scanned points into printable bodies; Steyerl converts the operational texture map into a political image of discontinuity; and Warburton reveals rendered visuality as an adjustable system of materials, shaders and parameters. The article argues that 3D formats shape contemporary visual culture by determining what spatial data can move between systems, by normalising the composite image as coherent visual output, and by producing format-specific residues that artists make available for critical perception. It extends format studies into 3D imaging and shows how artistic practice can operate as a media-archaeological method for examining computational images from within.

latest_articles.title: Responsibility vs. sensationalism: A cross-cultural review of media coverage of sexual violence
latest_articles.abstract: In this study, the media coverage of various incidents of sexual violence across the various countries of the world has been analyzed, and to surface that whether the media is responsible, sensational or neutral in coverage of such events. Media Coverage of sexual violence is examined in the context of Galdi and Guizzo (2021), the Media-Induced Sexual Harassment (MISH) framework and Simon and Gagnon (2003) Sexual Script Theory. The review suggests that sensationalized framing and sexually objectifying representations may reinforce harmful stereotypes, reduce empathy toward survivors, and contribute to public attitudes associated with sexual violence. Through a systematic search, the data was collected from major databases from 2012 to 2021 across major academic and open-access databases, including Google Scholar, PubMed, JSTOR, Web of Science, Sage Journals, and Library Genesis. Out of an initial pool of 172 potentially relevant research articles, the researchers identified and selected 135 articles that were most directly related to their specific research topic sexual violence against women for an in-depth, systematic review. The review indicates that sensational reporting remains more prevalent than responsible reporting across many cultural contexts, although important regional differences were identified.
affiliations: Department of Psychology, Ripha International University, Lahore, Pakistan
Huazhong University of Science and Technology

latest_articles.title: Ten years of the mobile world congress: Media impact on the city of Barcelona
latest_articles.abstract: The Mobile World Congress (MWC) has become an international benchmark in mobile technology and one of the most significant events hosted in Barcelona. Beyond its technological relevance, its media visibility may have played a key role in shaping the city’s public image and international reputation. This study aims to examine the impact of media coverage of the Mobile World Congress on the promotion and positioning of the city of Barcelona. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining content analysis and sentiment analysis through the implementation of a hierarchical multiclass automatic classification system. The study analysed news coverage published in three major regional newspapers— La Vanguardia , Ara.Cat , and El Periódico ( n = 3523 news articles). This methodological design enabled the identification of thematic patterns, dominant narratives, and the frequency with which Barcelona was associated with the event. The findings indicate that media coverage of the MWC has had a notably positive effect on Barcelona’s visibility and reputation. The newspapers consistently presented the city as a leading hub for technological innovation, international business, and large-scale global events. Recurrent references to Barcelona’s organisational capacity and strategic relevance within the mobile technology sector contributed to strengthening its urban brand and enhancing its symbolic capital in both regional and international media discourse. The MWC has significantly contributed to boosting and promoting the city of Barcelona. Media representation of the event has reinforced the city’s status as a global, innovation-driven urban centre and has consolidated its position within the international technological landscape.

latest_articles.title: Race, Ethnicity, Adaptation, Sitcom: The Finales of Seinfeld and Curb Your Enthusiasm
latest_articles.abstract: This article reads the finale of Curb Your Enthusiasm as an adaptation of the final double episode of Seinfeld . It argues that the continuities and differences between the two finales reflect a fundamental change in the comedic televisual representation of race, ethnicity and whiteness that points to broader historical transformations. Re-reading the Seinfeld finale from the perspective of sitcom, race and Jewishness, the article reveals a repressed racial subtext in the episode that complicates the Seinfeld characters’ whiteness through echoes of the televised murder trial of O. J. Simpson. This presence/absence dynamic of race and ethnicity is then made explicit, critiqued and subverted in Curb Your Enthusiasm ’s reinterpretation of the sitcom genre. Belatedly acknowledging Seinfeld’s and sitcom’s complicity in the exclusionary racial regime of 1990s television, Curb Your Enthusiasm explores alternative ways of representing and comically grappling with questions of racial and ethnic identity.
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong

latest_articles.title: “Anything is never enough”: strategic rhetoric in the socialization of new faculty members
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines faculty onboarding as a site of strategic rhetoric within the neoliberal university. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 30 faculty members across five cohorts (2019-2023), we investigate how organizational socialization practices designed to support new hires can reproduce opaque, ambiguous, and extractive institutional ideologies. Using de Certeau's [1984, The practice of everyday life (S. Rendall, Trans.). University of California Press] distinction between strategies and tactics, we analyze how institutions deploy rhetorics of individualism, victimization, and authenticity to resecure power and manage faculty labor, often at the expense of well-being. Findings show that formal onboarding programs struggle to counter these institutional forces. New faculty instead employ tactical communication, including building “shadow” systems of collective sensemaking, repurposing service for networking, and strategically complying with or resisting institutional demands to protect their professional integrity. We argue that faculty socialization is not a singular administrative event but a longitudinal pedagogical process through which faculty acquire and enact practical “counter-knowledge” for survival. We advocate faculty-led onboarding that develops critical literacy about institutional inequities and moves beyond transactional integration toward practices that protect faculty time, agency, and well-being within increasingly extractive academic systems.

latest_articles.title: Predicting Irritation Disclosures in Romantic Relationships: Testing and Extending the Revelation Risk Model
latest_articles.abstract: Feelings of irritation often emerge in romantic relationships. However, the theoretical mechanisms predicting whether individuals disclose these feelings to their romantic partner remain limited and largely reliant on examining indicators of future behavior rather than actual future behavior. Using a two-month, longitudinal survey design involving 448 participants, the current study tested the Revelation Risk Model (RRM) as a mechanism for predicting whether individuals would disclose or conceal feelings of irritation about their romantic partner. Relationship power was also incorporated as an additional predictor. The original RRM components (i.e., closeness, risk, communication efficacy, willingness to disclose) collectively predicted whether individuals disclosed or concealed feelings of irritation about their romantic partner. Relationship power predicted individuals’ communication efficacy, as well as perceived risk associated with disclosing their feelings of irritation. The findings are discussed in terms of their contributions to existing research on disclosure, irritations, and power in romantic relationships.
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, USA

latest_articles.title: Post hoc illusion—how the knew-it-all-along effect undermines trust
latest_articles.abstract: This article introduces a theory of distrust called the post hoc illusion. The post hoc illusion is a mistaken belief about what others knew in the past. It arises when stakeholders, who have entrusted power to the deciders, infer that the decider “overlooked” facts that were “obvious” and should have been consulted. We show how this effect is a logical consequence of constraints in human abductive processes–the manner in which human minds create and evaluate causal explanations. A research agenda for the post hoc illusion is then proposed, beginning with the identification of key variables that should influence its operation: relevant facts present in the past and theoretical novelty. We then argue that the illusion can be ameliorated through narratives that portray the decider’s state of mind in the past.
affiliations: Department of Communication, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York, United States
Department of Communication Science, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Amsterdam, Netherlands

latest_articles.title: Australian Cultural Policy and The Dame was Loaded (1996): A microhistorical account of a FMV movie game and the political promise of ‘multimedia’
latest_articles.abstract: ‘The interactive movie as a genre holds a place in the history of video games for one main reason: it’s a well-known failure,’ wrote Bernard Perron (2007:127) after conducting a comprehensive survey of work using full motion video (FMV) – or live action sequences – from the 1990s. Despite presenting a catalogue of their failings, Perron urges us not to dismiss these works but rather consider them as ‘experiments worth examining on their own terms’ (Perron et al., 2008:233). This paper revisits one such experiment: The Dame was Loaded (1996), by the Australian studio Beam Software that drew on the Hollywood conventions for detective movies and cinema noir. In this discussion we do not address the rhetorics of videogame histories' winners and losers, or the analysis of the formal qualities of FMV movie games which Perron et al. have exhaustively examined. Rather, we approach the work in the context of its historical status as being once championed as ‘Australia’s largest multimedia production.’ We examine the interactive movie game within the context of the promise of ‘multimedia’ and Australia’s political ambitions for developing its digital cultural industries in the 1990s. This more micro historical approach focuses on the place that the full motion video interactive movie The Dame was Loaded held in the vision for a multimedia future and addresses the FMV interactive movie experiment in terms of the local context of an arts and industry policy.

latest_articles.title: Identity-based digital deception in “visual-poverty” livestreams: A multimodal analysis
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines the emerging phenomenon of digital deception in “visual poverty” livestreams, with a particular focus on the strategic construction of fake identities. Drawing on a multimodal discourse analysis of livestream interactions, this study identifies three interrelated forms of fake identities: attribute identity, relational identity, and image identity. Of these, image identity emerges as the dominant mode of self-presentation, sustained and reinforced by the other two. These identities are further mediated through three key linguistic strategies: grammatical strategy, pragmatic strategy, and non-verbal strategy. The analysis demonstrates how livestream hosts deploy such strategies to shape viewer perceptions and build deceptive credibility. This study also discusses the challenges of detecting such identity manipulation in real-time mediated interactions and offers theoretical insights and practical implications for understanding and addressing digital deception.
affiliations: School of Foreign Languages and Cultures, Nanjing Normal University

latest_articles.title: Weekly Gaming Duration and Internet Gaming Disorder in Relation to Depression and Loneliness: A Two-Year Follow-Up Study
latest_articles.abstract: The current study examined the association between weekly video game engagement and mental health, specifically Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD), loneliness, and depression. We recruited 377 U.S. adults through CloudResearch Connect using gaming-frequency quotas, resulting in a sample representing a wide range of weekly gaming duration (range = 0–80 hours, M = 14.62). Analyses revealed that weekly gameplay hours did not consistently predict depression and loneliness. In contrast, people with higher IGD scores tended to have higher weekly playtime, more depressive symptoms, and greater feelings of loneliness. We readministered the same survey 2 years later ( N = 172 or 45.6 percent of baseline sample). Here, we found that both higher weekly hours and higher IGD scores at baseline predicted increases in depressive symptoms 2 years later, controlling for their baseline depression. We did not find that gaming was predictive of loneliness longitudinally. These findings are particularly relevant given the American Psychiatric Association’s interest in IGD in the DSM-5 coupled with the ongoing public debate about the benefits and ills of video games. Our findings suggest that people who struggle to balance gaming with other life demands may experience more depressive symptoms over time. Thus, clinicians may opt to focus on helping clients with IGD better balance their priorities.
affiliations: Department of Psychology, University of San Francisco, San Francisco, California, USA.

latest_articles.title: ‘But, today, you’ve got to be beyond reasonable doubt’: The discursive negotiation of judicial directions in mock-jury deliberations in England and Wales
latest_articles.abstract: Drawing on a corpus of mock-jury deliberations from England and Wales comprising 94,000 words of transcript and 10 hours of video data from 132 participants, this study employs discourse analysis – specifically interactional analysis and narrative analysis – to examine how mock jurors interpret, negotiate, and recontextualise judicial directions. The analysis identifies two interactional manifestations of juror agency: adherence to judicial directions, and transgression through lay-knowledge-based reasoning. These orientations reveal how mock jurors construct and contest interactional roles, manage intra-group dynamics, and navigate the relationship between everyday knowledge and institutional authority. Rather than depicting jurors as passive recipients of legal expertise, the study foregrounds their evidential reasoning, moral judgement, and interpretive agency. The findings contribute to discourse studies by bridging institutional discourse, epistemic agency, and the revalorisation of lay knowledge within courtroom interaction.

latest_articles.title: Predicting Symptom Change in Mental Health Chatbot Interventions: A Meta-Analysis
latest_articles.abstract: Mental health-focused chatbots have emerged as scalable interventions that deliver therapeutic content through conversational interfaces. This meta-analysis of 35 studies (N = 1,780) indicates that chatbots can reduce depression (g = -.53, 95% CI [−.67,-.40]) and anxiety (g = -.36, 95% CI [−.46,-.27]) symptoms over time. However, wide prediction intervals reveal substantial heterogeneity, suggesting that while some interventions are associated with symptom reduction, others may increase them. Moderator analyses revealed that therapeutic alliance significantly predicted reductions in both depression and anxiety symptoms. Task and goal alliance significantly predicted a reduction in depression symptoms, while bond alliance did not. Similarly, treatment acceptability significantly moderated depression symptom change, noting the importance of perceived intervention appropriateness. Mental health chatbots designed using cognitive behavioral therapy and interventions delivered over longer durations were associated with larger symptom reductions, particularly for anxiety. In addition, populations with both clinical and self-reported diagnoses were associated with larger reductions in depression symptoms compared to interventions recruiting general populations. Findings also reveal considerable gaps in mental health chatbot development and evaluation, as few studies have examined key communication-related moderators, such as therapeutic alliance and acceptability, despite their demonstrated importance in the mental health communication and therapeutic literature.

latest_articles.title: Afterword: the waning power of the fix
latest_articles.abstract: This commentary offers some reflections on the ‘power of the fix' in cybersecurity and its wider implications for technological democracy. I begin with a discussion of the discrepancy between the discourse of solutionism and everyday practices of securing IT systems (Elgaard Jensen et al, 2026). Whereas the former posits that problems are neat and can be solved by means of technology, the latter must confront what Röhle (2021) has called the ‘permanent brokenness' of computational infrastructures. A peculiar form of ‘infrastructural reversal' can then be observed in the field of cybersecurity: here, disruption, breakdown and failure are not the exception, but the default (Collier et al, 2025; Fouad, 2025). This has implications for the role of public disclosure of technological vulnerabilities in the governance of digital systems (Bozzini, 2025). The endemic nature of disruption in computational infrastructures puts at risk the transformative capacities of publicity in technological politics. This also affects social studies of technology insofar as this field has long relied on disruption, failure and breakdown as empirical occasions for making visible how technology works and does not work in practice.
affiliations: Centre for Interdisciplinary Methodologies, University of Warwick, Coventry, UK

latest_articles.title: Digital responsibility, skills and environmental awareness for digital sustainability
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigates how digital competencies and environmental awareness interact to shape eco-friendly digital practices, contributing to the field of digital sustainability. Drawing on a representative sample of adult internet users in the United Arab Emirates (N = 1016), it explores (H1) whether individual responsibility predicts environmentally conscious digital practices; (H2) whether environmental awareness moderates the effect of perceived digital competence on behavior; and (H3) whether sustainable digital behaviors are associated with perceived digital competence, with awareness as a moderator. Using linear and moderated regression analyses, the findings confirm that individual responsibility is a significant predictor of pro-environmental digital behavior, and that perceived digital competence is positively associated with such behavior, an association that is modestly strengthened, rather than enabled, by environmental awareness. The reverse association, from behavior to perceived digital competence, is not moderated by awareness, pointing to an asymmetrical pattern that the cross-sectional design does not allow us to interpret causally. By integrating digital inequality frameworks with environmental psychology, this study advances the understanding of digital sustainability as a site where perceived competence and responsibility jointly shape sustainable digital engagement.

latest_articles.title: Guidance over guidelines? Unpacking the uses and concerns of generative AI in communication science
latest_articles.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) tools has transformed research practices across communication science. As genAI tools (and most notetably large language models), made the generation of text, images, and other media content extremely easy, they can potentially disrupt the way science is conducted. Yet, their integration into academic workflows has outpaced systematic understanding of how, when, and why researchers use them. Drawing on a quantitative survey of N = 1138 communication scientists and four qualitative focus groups, this study provides the first comprehensive mapping of genAI use across communucation research stages and contexts. Findings reveal three key dynamics: a paradox between widespread use and persistent concern; conflicting expectations among individual scholars, institutions, and journals; and the influence of cultural and linguistic contexts on adoption patterns. Together, these findings highlight a multi-level governance challenge encompassing individual, institutional, and disciplinary dimensions. With this paper, we seek to provide a starting point for an open and transparent discussion about the role of generative AI in communication research by proposing a structured set of recommendations for responsible genAI use at three levels: field-wide coordination and collaboration, institutional guidance and support, and individual continuous critical reflection.
affiliations: Department of Communication and Technology, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Hsinchu, Taiwan
Amsterdam School of Communication Research, University of Amsterdam, Amsterdam, The Netherlands
School of Governance, Utrecht University, Utrecht, The Netherlands
Department of Language, Literature and Communication, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Amsterdam, The Netherlands

latest_articles.title: How Influencer Follower-Scale Popularity Erodes Luxury Brand Exclusivity: The Crowd Dilutes the Crown: How Micro-Influencers Reduce Social Crowding and Preserve Exclusivity
latest_articles.abstract: Influencer marketing is common in luxury branding, yet how influencer follower-scale popularity (macro vs. micro) shapes perceived brand exclusivity remains underexplored. Across five studies, four experiments and a field test, we show that micro-influencers increase purchase and brand usage intentions by reducing perceived social crowding and strengthening perceived brand exclusivity. We identify boundary conditions: the exclusivity-based pathway is stronger among consumers higher in Consumer Need for Uniqueness (CNFU), whereas both indirect pathways attenuate under luxury fatigue. The findings advance theory on diffusion cues and crowding in luxury contexts and offer guidance for influencer-tier selection when exclusivity is central.

latest_articles.title: How Information-Use Transparency Affects the Effectiveness of Location Targeting: When Privacy Disclosures Help and When They Backfire
latest_articles.abstract: Targeted advertising can increase ad effectiveness through personalization but may also evoke privacy concerns. Using two online experiments and a field experiment, this research examines how location targeting specificity and information-use transparency affect consumers’ click intentions and actual click behavior. Results show that more specific location targeting increases perceived personalization and consumer engagement. Consumers simultaneously weigh perceived personal relevance against perceived privacy intrusiveness when deciding whether to engage with an advertisement. The effects of transparency are context dependent: transparency mitigates privacy-related avoidance under less specific targeting, but increases privacy concerns when highly specific targeting makes personal data use particularly salient.Management SlantMore specific location targeting increases consumers’ overall intention to click and click behavior.Consumers’ clicking intentions reflect a tradeoff between perceived relevance and perceived privacy intrusiveness.Information-use transparency has a nuanced effect; failing to provide consumers with transparency increases the negative effect of perceived privacy intrusiveness and thereby reduces intention to click.Advertisers should calibrate transparency to the level of targeting specificity rather than treating transparency disclosures as universally beneficial.
affiliations: Institute of Electronic Commerce and Digital Markets, LMU Munich School of Management, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München

latest_articles.title: Massive Advertising Expenses Changes, Risk, and Implications for Stock Returns
latest_articles.abstract: This research paper offers a new analysis of the impact of U.S. firms’ expenses on advertising on the cross-section of stock returns. Rather than exploring the level of advertising expenses, this study concentrates on their logarithmic percentage change to emphasize only major changes. Massive negative changes present a risk and therefore account for higher stock returns. This impact is economically and statistically significant. Moreover, this impact is validated in various robustness tests. The analysis is performed on 231,323 U.S. firm-year observations. Researchers and practitioners can benefit from the analysis. Advertising management and advertisers should adjust advertising budgets gradually because massive declines are adverse for risk and cost of equity.
affiliations: Department of Economics and Business Administration, Ariel University

latest_articles.title: The Conformity Effects of Personalized Advertising: When Consumers Seek Social Anonymity
latest_articles.abstract: Personalized advertising has become a dominant strategy on social media, leveraging personal data to deliver tailored content. However, this practice raises privacy concerns by making data collection more noticeable. This research examines how personalized advertising influences conformity behaviors. Across seven experiments, we demonstrate that personalized advertising increases privacy concern, which in turn heightens the need for social anonymity and subsequently prompts conformity behaviors. Additionally, we investigate how perceived self-control capacity moderates this effect and examine how surveillance cues can help marketers design more effective strategies.

latest_articles.title: Whisper Sounds Become Mindful Relaxation: A Computational Analysis of Consumer Responses to ASMR Advertising
latest_articles.abstract: This research examines consumers’ responses to ASMR advertising and investigates the role of gendered brand personality in shaping immersion- and sexualization-oriented discourse within consumer–brand conversations. Using a computational text-mining approach, it analyzes 15,807 YouTube comments on ASMR advertising for masculine and feminine brands. Six topics emerged, including sexualized whisper cues, mindful relaxation, purchase discussion, hand-sound triggers, sleep-related immersion, and audience reactions. Feminine brands are associated with higher immersion scores, whereas masculine brands are associated with more sexualization-oriented discourse. The findings suggest that integrating sensory marketing and gendered brand personality with computational analysis helps explain divergent interpretations of ASMR advertising.

latest_articles.title: Feeling the crisis, building the alternative: Women journalists in nonprofit digital media through the lens of feminist epistemology and the affective turn
latest_articles.abstract: This article draws on feminist standpoint epistemology and the affective turn to examine how women journalists respond to deteriorating working conditions in Slovenian legacy media. The study focuses on three analytically selected cases of women journalists who co-founded nonprofit, women-led digital media outlets, drawn from 15 exploratory autobiographical interviews. Their narratives articulate experiences of marginalization alongside agentic responses that critically interrogate developments in the legacy media system and call for a rethinking of journalistic ethics and labor organization. Journalism is approached as affective labor, marked by the entanglement of passion, self-exploitation, and precarity, in which emotions such as anger, care, and responsibility – combined with digital affordances – enable the creation of alternative media spaces. These initiatives are interpreted not merely as individual survival strategies but as micropolitical and epistemological interventions that reclaim professional autonomy and integrity. While embedded in neoliberal conditions and structurally fragile, they demonstrate the potential of alternative practices to reimagine journalism from the margins.
affiliations: The Peace Institute, Institute for Contemporary Social and Political Studies, Ljubljana, Slovenia

latest_articles.title: Explaining Science Knowledge Gaps on Social Media: Basic Science Knowledge and Intentional Versus Incidental Exposure
latest_articles.abstract: This study examined whether basic science knowledge helps explain education-based gaps in domain-specific science knowledge and whether intentional and incidental exposure on social media condition those gaps. A national survey of American adults focused on two domains: climate change and algorithms. Results showed that basic science knowledge mediated the relationship between education and domain-specific knowledge across both domains. These indirect relationship were attenuated at higher levels of intentional social media exposure. The findings suggest that strengthening foundational science literacy and encouraging more deliberate engagement with science content on social media may help reduce knowledge disparities.
affiliations: Stony Brook University, New York﻿, USA

latest_articles.title: mlstats : An R Package for Multilevel Descriptive Statistics and Data Preparation
latest_articles.abstract: Mobile research methods such as experience sampling, smartphone logging, and daily diary designs produce nested data, in which within-level fluctuations must be distinguished from between-level differences. Yet, there is no established convention for preparing and descriptively reporting such multilevel data. This paper introduces mlstats , an open-source R package that computes multilevel descriptive statistics—including intraclass correlation coefficients and within- and between-group correlations—in a single call, exports publication-ready tables, and decomposes variables for random effects within-between modeling. Supporting both frequentist and Bayesian estimation, mlstats is freely available on Comprehensive R Archive Network with extensive online documentation at https://felixdidi.github.io/mlstats/ .

latest_articles.title: With Great Power Comes Great Complexity: A Psycholinguistic and Rhetorical Analysis of Gender in Superhero Movies
latest_articles.abstract: This study utilizes integrative complexity (IC), a psycholinguistic/rhetorical construct that measures structural nuance in communication, to analyze gender, character role, and critical response in superhero films. Sampled dialogue from superheroes and supervillains across critically acclaimed and critically panned movies was collected/analyzed; while ANOVAs revealed no significant main effects for character role and critical response, a significant main effect for gender was found. As expected, the female characters—both superheroes and supervillains—demonstrated lower IC levels than their male counterparts, indicating that they are less focused/emphasized during creation and are positioned as reactionary/subordinate. Prior research spotlights the shortcomings of gender in superhero cinema, and while some scholars argue for female superheroes’ transgressive potential, these results suggest that potential has not been achieved.

latest_articles.title: Democratic Media Performance and Democratization: A Global Longitudinal Perspective
latest_articles.abstract: Media that effectively perform their democratic functions are widely considered a key driver of democratization, yet longitudinal evidence on their impact remains limited. This study analyzed global annual time-series data on democratic media performance and democratization from 1946 to 2018. ARIMA models indicated a covariation between annual increases in democratic media performance and gains in democratization worldwide, measured by Vanhanen’s Index of Democratization. The analysis also revealed covariation with V-Dem’s liberal, participatory, deliberative, and egalitarian component indices of democratic quality. Evidence on temporal ordering, consistent with Granger causality, was found for Vanhanen’s index and the participatory and deliberative V-Dem component indices; evidence was marginal for the liberal component and absent for the egalitarian component. Acknowledging limitations regarding causal interpretation, the results are consistent with the claim that media can act as a leading force in democratic development rather than merely reflecting it, particularly in electoral, participatory, and deliberative dimensions.

latest_articles.title: Archives of power: Algorithmic memory, ideological (Re)production and negotiation of hegemonic masculinity
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines how algorithmic memory shapes the production and negotiation of masculinity in the context of Nigeria. Inductively adopting Connell’s theory of hegemonic masculinity as an interpretive framework, the article attempts to understand how digital platforms mediate men’s self-perceptions amid economic precarities and shifting gender expectations. The analysis of two focus group discussions with men aged 24 to 45, the author constructed three interrelated dynamics: Algorithmic temporal dislocation (How resurfaced memories evoke shame and anxiety over economic failure); Memory curation as counter-memory (Strategies to reassert agency over algorithmic authorship and dominance); and Platformed provision and performing masculinity (Online visibility as a performative substitute for material provision), which explain how algorithmic systems shape and reproduce ideals of hegemonic masculinity. By locating algorithmic memory within the cultural politics of masculinity in Africa, this article advances our understanding of digital media as spaces where algorithms shape whose memories are amplified, whose identities are recognized, and how existing gender and social inequalities are reproduced and contested.
affiliations: Department of Sociology, University of Toronto

latest_articles.title: Fan translation as memetic communication: Understanding cultural diffusion through cross-cultural fan labour
latest_articles.abstract: This article explores the role of online fan translation in the cross-cultural consumption and dissemination of popular culture through a case study of the production and reproduction of translated K-pop content across different genres and platforms. It proposes memetic communication as a conceptual framework for understanding cultural diffusion through fan translation. While internet memes are recognised as a ubiquitous digital media practice, this study attempts to theorise memetic communication as a vital mode of online communication that penetrates various kinds of content reproduction and audience engagement in popular culture, with a focus on fan translation. More specifically, this article illustrates how memetic communication – that is, cultural reproduction driven by creative imitation and manipulation – is akin to fan translation, which often involves innovative remediation practices and grassroots distribution. It also investigates how translation can be an integral part of broader memetic communication by establishing textual relationships with other content, including that which is fan-produced. This study’s key argument is that translation permeates the different processes of content production and dissemination, thereby facilitating cultural diffusion.

latest_articles.title: The Heritage Heuristic: Strategic Benefits of Organizational Heritage Communication in Managing Negative Publicity
latest_articles.abstract: Successfully managing negative publicity is challenging, which is why organizations require effective communication strategies to mitigate adverse outcomes. Previous research indicates that one such strategy is emphasizing a long history tied to the issue. Building on the heuristics literature, this paper innovatively examines whether perceptions of an organization’s overall history, not just its issue-specific past, can provide protection against negative publicity, as history-related perceptions may trigger automatic, meaningful judgments about the organization. In a preregistered experiment (N = 600, representative Dutch sample), we measured participants’ organizational heritage perceptions, which refers to stakeholders’ shared understanding of an organization’s historical roots, legacy, and enduring values, of a fictional brand with varying years of establishment. Half of them next read a negative publicity article about the brand accusing it of unethical behavior. We found that heritage perceptions (longevity, continuity, tradition, adaptability) reduced negative brand-related emotions and cognitions, and that perceived authenticity appeared to function as a mediator. Our findings suggest that emphasizing organizational heritage could be an important tool for organizations when responding to negative publicity. This paper thereby establishes the ‘heritage heuristic’ as one that deserves more scholarly attention in strategic communication research in the future.

latest_articles.title: Generative AI Disclosure in Advertising: From Intent- to Production-Based Disclosure
latest_articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming advertising production and introducing new forms of disclosure at the point of exposure. Existing research treats disclosure primarily as a cue signaling persuasive intent, yet GenAI disclosures increasingly communicate how content was produced rather than why it was created. This paper reconceptualizes disclosure in AI-mediated advertising by positioning GenAI disclosure as a signal of production conditions. Integrating signaling theory, source credibility theory, the persuasion knowledge model, and the heuristic–systematic model, the paper develops a conceptual framework that differentiates declarative, regulatory, and infrastructural disclosure as distinct rendering conditions. The framework proposes that GenAI disclosure influences consumer evaluations through two complementary inferential pathways: perceived source attribution and production-based agent knowledge, defined as consumers’ beliefs about how persuasive content was generated and what those production processes imply for evaluating the persuasion agent. It further specifies how consumers’ motivation and ability shape the likelihood of heuristic versus systematic processing. The paper advances advertising theory by explaining how disclosure operates when its primary referent shifts from persuasive intent to production conditions and by providing a framework for understanding why similar disclosure cues may generate divergent evaluative responses across consumers, contexts, and forms of GenAI use.

latest_articles.title: Should Ads Be Assertive? A Meta-Analytic Review of the Effects of Assertive Language on Perceived Freedom Threat, State Reactance, and Persuasion Outcomes
latest_articles.abstract: Advertising messages often use assertive language to capture consumer attention and drive behavioral compliance, yet empirical evidence for its effectiveness remains inconclusive and contradictory across studies and contexts. This meta-analytic review synthesized 142 samples examining the effects of assertive language in advertising messages on perceived freedom threat, state reactance, and persuasion outcomes. Drawing on psychological reactance theory, we used meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) to conduct the first test in the reactance literature of a serial mediation model in which assertive language first increases perceived freedom threat, which subsequently heightens state reactance, ultimately reducing persuasive effectiveness. Overall, assertive language significantly increased perceived freedom threat (d = 0.72) and state reactance (d = 0.39), while demonstrating a small but significant negative effect on persuasion outcomes (d = −0.08). Importantly, MASEM provided evidence that the effect of assertive language on persuasion outcomes was serially mediated through perceived threat to freedom and state reactance. Moderation analyses revealed that advertising domain significantly moderated the effect on state reactance, with nonprofit contexts eliciting stronger reactance responses than for-profit contexts. These findings clarify the mechanism of psychological reactance in advertising and provide clear guidance for advertisers on when and why to avoid assertive language.

latest_articles.title: Governmental Public Health Must Strengthen Its Strategic Communications Infrastructure — Not Just Training
latest_articles.abstract: Scientific expertise, policy change, and community engagement are commonly understood as the primary tools of governmental public health. The COVID-19 pandemic made it clear that communications is also a core function. It also exposed the severe constraints of governmental public health's current communications capacity: inconsistent funding, understaffed teams, narrow authority within agencies, and an overreliance on dissemination-focused roles. Together, these constraints leave public health communications poorly equipped for today's environment. Public health agencies and funders typically address gaps in communications capacity by emphasizing training programs to build individual skills. While necessary, this emphasis is insufficient. We review evidence to suggest that the most persistent challenges facing governmental public health communications result not from individual skill gaps, but from underinvestment in communications infrastructure. Without sustained investment in leadership roles, workforce pathways, and narrative capacity, training alone cannot enable communications to best serve the needs of our communities' health. We deliberately use the plural "communications" to signal organizational function, distinguishing it from the singular communication infrastructure of communities described in the broader literature. Together with other communications leaders in Big Cities Health Coalition member health departments, we have begun to outline a strategic vision for local government public health communications. In this perspective piece, we outline our initial thinking about how to move our field forward strategically.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Which Way Does Cupid’s Arrow Go? Distinguishing Happiness and Meaningfulness Within Romantic Relationships
latest_articles.abstract: Happiness and meaningfulness are viewed as distinct aspects of psychological wellbeing, but their role in romantic relationships remains unknown. In two online studies, we sought to identify key differences between people’s judgments of relationship happiness and meaningfulness. Study 1 ( n = 426) found that greater sexual desire and satisfaction, and fewer relationship sacrifices and less stress, contributed to relationship happiness but were unconnected to relationship meaningfulness. By contrast, greater negative self-disclosure to one’s partner predicted relationship meaningfulness but was unlinked to relationship happiness. Study 2 ( n = 711) successfully replicated these findings, and further showed that people who prefer a meaningful relationship (over a happy one) exhibit a more favorable psychosocial profile, including greater relationship satisfaction, optimism, interpersonal closeness, forgiveness, and less relationship stress. These studies are the first to show that a distinct profile of psychosocial correlates distinguishes happy from meaningful romantic relationships, and they highlight the need for future research to consider hedonic and eudaimonic elements in relationship processes separately.
affiliations: Department of Psychology, University of Toronto

latest_articles.title: Affective journalism and identity: Community newspapers as emotional agents in Hong Kong
latest_articles.abstract: Situated within Hong Kong’s rapidly shifting sociopolitical context and complex identity landscape, this article examines how community newspapers produce community imaginaries in Hong Kong, focusing on the affective-discursive strategies through which grassroots journalism constructs community knowledge. Treating emotion as an epistemic infrastructure, this article draws on affective epistemology to examine how such strategies in two ideologically divergent community newspapers constitute distinct forms of community knowledge for readers. Through a comparative critical discourse analysis of one pro-democracy and one pro-establishment community newspaper, the analysis identifies two distinct affective strategies: an affective-participatory strategy that constitutes community as a self-determining collective subject, and an affective-governance strategy that constitutes community as a condition of harmony sustained through virtuous individuals and aligned institutions.

latest_articles.title: Reasserting the Relevance of Media Trust: A Response to Jakobsson and Stiernstedt (2023)
latest_articles.abstract: This article responds to Jakobsson and Stiernstedt's (2023. “Trust and the media: Arguments for the (irr)elevance of a concept.” Journalism Studies 24 (4): 479–495) invitation to critically examine the significance of media trust. They argue that there “is a lack of strong arguments for why falling levels of trust in the news media are legitimately described as a crisis or problem” (479). Their critique offers a valuable counterpoint to the (often implicit) assumption that news media trust is always positive. Still, I argue for closer examination of their central arguments to move toward a comprehensive synthesis. I draw on political science literature and research on the consequences of media trust to reassert the importance of media trust for news consumption, democracy and ontological security. Without a comprehensive synthesis, debate over media trust risks becoming polarized and binary, with scholars selectively citing research that supports their views. The paperproposes two ways forward. First, a dynamic conceptualization of media trust similar to a “thermostat” where media trust provides a baseline openness to information, while vigilance operates as an adaptive regulator, selectively heightening scrutiny. Second, combining cultural and institutional perspectives to develop a more nuanced understanding of the significance of media trust.

latest_articles.title: Inspirational Olympic Stories: Exploring the Impact of Athlete Identity Framing and Superordinate Identity on Feelings of National Identity, Elevation, Admiration, and Grit
latest_articles.abstract: Major sporting events like the Olympics serve as symbolic arenas for national identity construction and emotional engagement. This two-study experimental investigation examined how media portrayals of Olympic athletes influence audience responses depending on the framing of intended inspirational audience and athlete identity. Grounded in social identity theory and the common ingroup identity model, Study 1 (n = 139) tested whether framing an athlete as aiming to inspire a superordinate national audience (i.e. “young Americans”) versus a specific subgroup (i.e. “young Latinos”) influenced readers’ feelings of national identity, elevation, and grit. Study 2 (n = 157) tested whether identifying an athlete as “American” versus “Mexican-American” affected admiration and grit. Results from Study 1 indicated that superordinate identity framing elicited higher national identity, elevation, and grit, while results from Study 2 showed that identifying an athlete according to a superordinate identity was associated with higher levels of admiration, with admiration mediating the relationship between identity framing and grit. These findings demonstrate that emphasizing inclusive national identities in media narratives fosters more positive emotional and motivational responses among audiences. Implications are discussed regarding the role of inspirational sports media in shaping collective identity and promoting prosocial emotional experiences during major international events.

latest_articles.title: Political Endorsements by TikTok Influencers: Parasocial Interaction, Identification, and Support for Political Candidates
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines political persuasion on TikTok by testing how influencers’ direct address and media source labels shape audience responses to a political endorsement video. Using a preregistered 2 × 2 online survey experiment with 486 U.S. adults, we found that participants exposed to direct address, defined as the influencer looking directly at the camera, reported significantly higher identification with the influencer and stronger parasocial interaction than those exposed to non-direct address. Drawing on the Entertainment Overcoming Resistance Model, mediation analyses further showed that direct address indirectly increased intention to support the endorsed political candidate through multiple relational and cognitive pathways, including identification, parasocial interaction, counterarguing, perceived norms, and perceived video credibility. By contrast, media source labels did not significantly affect perceived video credibility, did not indirectly influence candidate support, and did not moderate the effects of direct address. These findings point to the importance of relational cues in short-form political influencer communication. By identifying the mechanisms through which influencer content affects attitudes and behavioral intentions, this study advances theory on entertainment-based persuasion and provides practical insights into political communication and influencer politics in short-form media environments.
